Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.

## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

This is a technical spec document — the right treatment is utilitarian but polished: clear typographic hierarchy, a considered palette drawn from the subject (biotech/clinical data, cartographic framing), and layout that makes a dense spec scannable. No hero flourishes; the craft goes into structure, readability, and information density.

**Design plan:**
- **Color**: `#0D1117` near-black ground with a slight blue-black bias; `#F0F4F8` off-white text (cool, not cream); `#2D6A9F` slate-blue primary accent (clinical, cartographic); `#4BBFA0` teal secondary (data/output nodes); `#C97D3A` amber warning/unknown state; `#1A2332` mid-ground for code blocks and callout panels
- **Type**: `ui-monospace` / system mono for code, paths, schema — the spec is deeply technical and mono should feel native, not a novelty; `system-ui` for body and headers — neutral delivery, hierarchy through weight and size only; no display face needed here
- **Layout**: single-column with a sticky section nav rail on left at wider viewports; sections numbered as a true sequence (the spec sections are genuinely ordered); generous leading in body, tight in code/schema blocks

Objective Produce a static, file://-openable HTML+SVG disease landscape map for **type 2 diabetes mellitus** (MONDO:0005148) that communicates competitive structure, mechanism coverage, and data-quality state to an investment analyst without requiring a server, framework, or live data connection. The map is a diagnostic visualization only — its purpose is to make the shape of the T2DM competitive landscape legible and to surface where the current data pipeline is blind (stage, mechanism). Output is a self-contained directory of four files generated by a single Python script that reads existing diagnostic artifacts. No portfolio signals, no scoring integration, no production wiring. --- ## 2. Input Artifacts All files are under: `artifacts/scientific_cartography/2026-06-23/` (absolute: `/mnt/c/Projects/biotech_screener/biotech-screener/artifacts/scientific_cartography/2026-06-23/`) | File | Role in map | Known quality issues | |---|---|---| | `map_index.json` | Disease-level summary: program count, ticker list, cluster count, known_mechanism_count, source_refs_count, stage_distribution. Primary selection and metadata source. | `stage_distribution` is 100% unknown for all diseases — `phase`→`phases` field name mismatch in `_parse_simplified_format`. Not fixed in R2. `therapeutic_area` is null for all entries. | | `competitive_clusters.jsonl` | Cluster records for T2DM: mechanism_class, modality, target, program_count, public_tickers, asset_names, source_refs, warnings. Defines the horizontal layout of the map. | 3 of 3 MONDO:0005148 clusters have `clinical_stage_bucket: null` and `confidence: 0.0`. Two mechanism clusters (GLP-1 RA, TNF inhibitor) have real mechanism data; the third (1,041 programs) is `unknown\|unknown\|unknown`. All `phase*_count` fields are 0. | | `landscape_features.jsonl` | Per-program feature records for T2DM (1,046 records): asset_name, ticker, mechanism_class, modality, source_refs, public_program_count, warnings. Used to populate node content and source-ref counts. | `clinical_stage: null` on all 1,046 features. `mechanism_crowding_score`, `stage_crowding_score`, `white_space_score`, `differentiation_proxy_score` all null. `feature_confidence: 0.0` on all records. | | `artifact_manifest.json` | Governance attestation and input/output file registry. Used to embed provenance in map footer. | None. | | `scientific_cartography_status.json` | Run-level status: success/fail, warnings, errors, artifact list. Used to render data-quality banner. | None — run was clean (0 warnings, 0 errors). | **Critical constraint:** Because `clinical_stage` is null on all records, the map cannot place programs in a stage-based column layout. The fallback column scheme is defined in Section 5. --- ## 3. Disease Selection **Selected disease: type 2 diabetes mellitus (MONDO:0005148)** Evidence from the 2026-06-23 diagnostic run: - **Program count:** 1,046 — 6th-largest disease in the index; materially smaller than lymphoma (5,495) and breast cancer (2,340) but large enough to be representative - **Ticker count:** 53 public tickers — broad universe coverage; non-oncology disease, so program-per-ticker ratio is lower and asset identities are more distinct - **Cluster count:** 3 competitive clusters in MONDO:0005148. Two have real mechanism data (GLP-1 receptor agonist / small molecule / GLP1R; TNF inhibitor / monoclonal antibody / TNF). The third cluster groups the 1,041 mechanism-unknown programs. - **Known mechanism count:** 5 programs with known mechanism (out of 1,046 = 0.48%); highest non-oncology count in the disease index after lymphoma (13) - **Source refs count:** 513 distinct ClinicalTrials.gov NCT IDs — strong source anchoring for the 200-program `Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2` sub-entity; 1,046 total features across 513 refs - **Rationale over lymphoma/breast cancer:** Oncology diseases accumulate programs through broad basket-trial designs, artificially inflating program counts. T2DM has a well-understood competitive structure (GLP-1, SGLT2, insulin, TNF — even if the normalizer only resolves two of these currently) that makes cluster interpretation meaningful independent of stage data. **Stage data state:** 100% unknown for all 1,046 T2DM programs. This is a system-wide issue (field name mismatch: `phase` vs `phases`, `status` vs `overall_status` in `_parse_simplified_format` in `ctgov_ingest.py`). The prototype must surface this prominently and use a fallback column scheme. The reader must not be misled into thinking stage data exists. --- ## 4. Output Files All output files under: `artifacts/scientific_cartography/map_ux/type-2-diabetes-mellitus/` (absolute: `/mnt/c/Projects/biotech_screener/biotech-screener/artifacts/scientific_cartography/map_ux/type-2-diabetes-mellitus/`) | File | Description | |---|---| | `index.html` | Self-contained single-file page. Inlines `map.svg` directly in the DOM (not via ``). Includes: data-quality banner at top, disease header, mechanism legend, map viewport with SVG, data-provenance footer. Opens in browser with `file://` — no server, no external requests. All CSS and JS inline. | | `map.svg` | Standalone SVG file (also inlined in `index.html`). Contains the full landscape map — cluster lanes, program nodes, labels, axis annotations. Viewbox-scaled so it scrolls horizontally inside its container when content overflows. Must be valid standalone SVG. | | `map.json` | Machine-readable data contract. Full schema defined in Section 7. Contains the processed, filtered, and structured data that the SVG layout was built from. Enables reproducibility verification and future tooling. | | `README.md` | Human-readable run record: disease selected, input artifact paths, key counts, known data quality issues (stage null, mechanism sparse), date generated, governance attestation, next-step notes (stage fix in `ctgov_ingest.py`). | --- ## 5. Visual Grammar ### Map frame The map is organized as a **two-axis grid**: - **Rows (Y-axis / lanes):** Mechanism classes. One lane per distinct mechanism class found in the competitive clusters, ordered by program count descending. An additional final lane labeled **"[mechanism unknown]"** holds all programs where `mechanism_class` is null. - **Columns (X-axis):** Stage is 100% unknown, so the fallback column scheme uses **source-ref count** as a proxy for evidence depth. Programs are binned into three columns: - **"Single source"** — `source_refs_count == 1` - **"Multi-source (2–9)"** — `source_refs_count` between 2 and 9 - **"Deep evidence (10+)"** — `source_refs_count >= 10` Each column is labeled with its bin definition. A prominent banner above the map reads: **"Stage data unresolved — columns show source-ref depth, not clinical stage. See Implementation Notes."** The column headers are rendered in amber to signal the fallback state, not the intended design. ### Node encoding Each node represents one program (one row in `landscape_features.jsonl` for the target disease). | Visual property | Encoding | |---|---| | **Shape** | Circle for all nodes in this prototype. Modality distinction is deferred until mechanism normalizer coverage improves. | | **Size** | Fixed radius for all individual program nodes. Cluster summary nodes (one per cluster in the mechanism legend) are larger (2× radius). | | **Fill color** | Mechanism class drives hue: GLP-1 receptor agonist → blue-green; TNF inhibitor → amber-orange; unknown mechanism → slate-grey at 40% opacity. If future mechanism classes are present, assign from a fixed 6-color categorical palette, reserving grey for unknown. | | **Stroke** | Source-ref count drives stroke weight: 1 source → hairline (0.5px); 2–9 → medium (1.5px); 10+ → heavy (2.5px). Stroke color matches fill at higher saturation. | | **Opacity** | `feature_confidence == 0.0` → base opacity 0.55. When confidence > 0 (future state), opacity 0.9. This visually distinguishes the current all-zero confidence state from future improved data. | ### Label rules - **Cluster lane labels (row axis):** Mechanism class name, left-aligned, uppercase small caps, with program count in parentheses. Example: `GLP-1 RECEPTOR AGONIST (5)` / `[MECHANISM UNKNOWN] (1,041)`. - **Column headers:** Source-ref bin label, centered, with the amber warning treatment when stage is unresolved. - **Individual program node labels:** Ticker symbol only, rendered at 8px below each node, clipped if overlapping. Only render ticker label if the program's ticker appears in the screener universe (`public_tickers` from the cluster record). Non-universe tickers are unlabeled. - **Cluster summary callout:** For each named-mechanism cluster, render the asset names as a small tooltip-style text block anchored to the cluster's centroid. Include only the first three asset names, followed by "+ N more" if count exceeds three. ### Tooltip / sidecard content On hover/focus of a program node, reveal a sidecard panel (absolutely positioned, stays within viewport). Sidecard fields: - Asset name - Ticker (if universe member: bold; otherwise normal weight) - Mechanism class (or "[unknown]") - Modality (or "[unknown]") - Source refs: first three NCT IDs as links formatted as `NCT#######` (non-clickable in file:// context; rendered as monospace) - Source ref count: "N ClinicalTrials.gov records" - Feature confidence: rendered as a fraction-bar — e.g., "Confidence: 0.00" with a note "Low confidence — mechanism/stage data absent" - Warnings list from the feature record (comma-separated, rendered in amber) ### Unknown-state rendering Three distinct visual treatments for unknown/absent data: 1. **Stage unknown (system-wide):** Column axis replaced with source-ref proxy. Column headers rendered in amber with a warning icon (⚠). A non-dismissible banner appears above the map. 2. **Mechanism unknown (per-node):** Grey fill at 40% opacity. The `[mechanism unknown]` lane is visually separated from named-mechanism lanes by a 2px dashed row divider. Lane background is light grey, distinct from white named-mechanism lane backgrounds. 3. **Confidence zero (per-node):** Reduced node opacity (0.55). A legend entry reads: "Faded nodes = zero confidence (mechanism/stage data absent)". --- ## 6. Data Pipeline (no server) The generator script `tools/generate_scientific_cartography_map_ux.py` runs as a standalone CLI and produces the four output files. No server process, no live data access, no network calls. **Step 1 — Load inputs** Read from `artifacts/scientific_cartography/{as_of_date}/`: - Parse `map_index.json` → extract the entry for `disease_id == "MONDO:0005148"` → yields disease-level metadata (program_count, tickers, cluster_count, known_mechanism_count, source_refs_count, stage_distribution) - Stream `competitive_clusters.jsonl` → filter rows where `disease_id == "MONDO:0005148"` → yields 3 cluster records - Stream `landscape_features.jsonl` → filter rows where `disease_id == "MONDO:0005148"` → yields 1,046 feature records - Read `artifact_manifest.json` → yields governance block and input provenance - Read `scientific_cartography_status.json` → yields run status and warnings **Step 2 — Build the map data model** Construct the `MapData` structure (defined in Section 7): - `disease`: populated from map_index entry - `stage_resolved`: set `false` (confirmed: all stage values are 0) - `column_scheme`: set `"source_ref_depth"` since `stage_resolved == false` - `columns`: build three column definitions from source_ref bins [1, 2-9, 10+] - `mechanisms`: for each unique `mechanism_class` in cluster records (including null), create a `MechanismLane`. Sort: named mechanisms first by total `program_count` descending, then null/unknown lane last. - `programs`: for each landscape_feature record, compute: - `source_ref_count` from `len(source_refs)` on the feature record - `column_bucket` from the source_ref_count bin - `is_universe_member` from whether `ticker` appears in the disease's `public_tickers` list - `display_label` = ticker if `is_universe_member`, else empty string - All other fields pass through directly from the feature record **Step 3 — Layout algorithm** The SVG layout is computed in Python before writing the SVG — no JavaScript layout, all coordinates are burned into the SVG. - Define constants: `NODE_RADIUS = 7`, `NODE_MARGIN = 4`, `LANE_PADDING = 20`, `COLUMN_WIDTH = 240`, `LANE_LABEL_WIDTH = 220`, `HEADER_HEIGHT = 80` - For each mechanism lane, collect all programs in that lane and sort them by source_ref_count descending - Pack nodes within each lane×column cell using a simple row-wrap packing: place nodes left-to-right, wrap to next row when column width is reached - Compute cell height from the packed node count in that cell; lane height = max cell height across all three columns + `LANE_PADDING` - Assign each node an `(cx, cy)` coordinate in the SVG coordinate space - Total SVG height = sum of lane heights + `HEADER_HEIGHT`. Total SVG width = `LANE_LABEL_WIDTH + 3 * COLUMN_WIDTH` - Nodes for the mechanism-unknown lane are rendered identically but with grey fill and reduced opacity - Write coordinates to each program record in the `MapData` structure (adds `svg_cx`, `svg_cy` fields) **Step 4 — Render SVG** Produce the SVG as a string using Python string formatting (no SVG library needed; output is simple circles, text, and lines): - SVG root with `viewBox="0 0 {width} {height}"`, `width="100%"`, `height="{height}"`, `xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"` - Background rect for the full SVG - Column headers (3 text elements at x = lane_label_width + col_index * col_width + col_width/2) - For each mechanism lane: background rect (white or light-grey for unknown), left-edge lane label text, dashed separator line above unknown lane - For each program node: `` with computed cx/cy/r/fill/stroke/opacity, `data-feature-id` attribute for JS hover binding, and a `` child with the asset name (fallback tooltip) - Ticker labels: `<text>` below each labeled node - Source-ref depth legend in top-right corner (three circle examples at different stroke weights) - Mechanism color legend in top-left (below column headers) **Step 5 — Wrap in HTML** Build `index.html` as a single string: - `<title>T2DM Landscape Map — Scientific Cartography v0.2b (2026-06-23)` - Inline CSS: page layout, banner styles (amber for stage warning), sidecard panel (hidden by default), legend styles - Inline the SVG string directly in the `` (not via ``) so that JavaScript can attach hover handlers to SVG elements - Inline JavaScript: attach `mouseover`/`mouseout` listeners to all `` elements; on hover, populate sidecard from the `MAP_DATA` JS object (a JSON literal of the `programs` array written inline) and position the sidecard near the cursor; on mouseout, hide sidecard - Data quality banner: always-visible amber strip at top of page stating "Stage data unresolved — columns reflect source-ref depth.
